attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his essay, answering his own heading question.

semantics.note: The firm parts are present-tense: costs are not trending down and have not gone down yet. The 'maybe' only covers a possible future fall, and the claim keeps it as a qualifier. Calling this an observation is right.

contract.note: Counting token-inclusive cost for comparable work matches his own complaint about per-token comparisons, so it is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Has not gone down yet' is categorical, so a documented decline at fixed capability tests it fairly. The trend part is less precisely tied down.

evidence.note: Independent Epoch AI study (March 2025, inside the period). It uses recorded token counts and finds evaluation costs fell at fixed benchmark performance levels, roughly as fast as per-token prices. That is a token-inclusive decline during the period.

reviews.rationale: The contract counts the claim as contradicted if comparable token-inclusive costs fell during the period. Epoch's measurements meet that test: costs at fixed capability levels fell sharply, and faster after January 2024. This contradicts 'nor has it gone down yet.' The packet does not show the frontier-workload trend in August 2025, but the contract's either-or condition is already met.

attribution.note: Zitron presents this as his own calculation in his essay.

semantics.note: The claim keeps the 30% allocation assumption, the 2024-onward window and the $41.4B funding input. It is a bespoke estimate built on stated inputs.

contract.note: Checking the stated inputs and the arithmetic, and treating 30% as an assumption he disclosed, is fair to a self-described estimate. The open questions are which fiscal or calendar years the inputs cover and whether 'funding received' means money actually received.

evidence.note: The speaker's own essay. It reproduces the arithmetic (about 82.08) but cannot validate its own inputs.
CNBC reports that the $80B is Microsoft's fiscal-2025 plan, ending in June. This raises a possible overlap between periods but does not by itself show the input is materially wrong.
SoftBank's disclosure shows a staged, syndicated commitment of up to $40B. It does not establish how much OpenAI had actually received in total.

reviews.rationale: The arithmetic matches the stated inputs. No independent record in the packet confirms the $41.4B funding figure, and the Microsoft capex inputs have not been reconciled across fiscal and calendar years. The evidence neither validates the inputs nor shows they materially differ, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his essay.

semantics.note: An unhedged claim that inference cost has risen and that contrary claims are false. 'The opinion of somebody who does not know' is rhetoric and is rightly left out.

contract.note: Reading cost as token-inclusive spending per comparable unit of work in real applications fits his reasoning-token argument and is an ordinary reading. It neither stretches the claim nor turns it into a denial of every single price cut.

evidence.note: Cursor's own disclosure. Most users' costs stayed fairly constant, while the hardest requests cost far more. It is not a representative longitudinal trend.
OpenAI's own disclosure that GPT-4.1 is cheaper per median query than GPT-4o. This covers one vendor and one model pair, not representative application spending.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs representative longitudinal data on application spending. The packet has only two company disclosures pointing in mixed directions: Cursor reports flat costs for most users with costly hard requests, and OpenAI reports one cheaper model. Neither settles the general direction, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: 'Aren't going to be adopted' is a firm forecast with no deadline, so it is scored. The claim drops the 'many little distinct operations' premise, but that does not change the forecast.

contract.note: Reading 'mass-scale use' as substantial, sustained adoption for a major non-AI workload is ordinary. It is also fair that an open-ended negative forecast can only be contradicted early, never confirmed.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's August 2026 description of its cuDF analytics acceleration, with a few customer examples. It is vendor material and does not establish a mass-adoption milestone.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and failure to adopt so far cannot confirm it. The only evidence is a vendor claim about GPU analytics with a few customer examples, which falls short of the contract's documented mass-adoption milestone. With no conclusive event, the outcome is unresolved.
